chapter_title: Managing Local Storage with Partitions and Filesystems
chapter_summary:
Effective storage management begins with understanding how physical disks are organized and made accessible to the operating system. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux, this typically involves partitioning a disk and then creating a filesystem on those partitions. Historically, the Master Boot Record (MBR) partitioning scheme has been prevalent, supporting up to four primary partitions or three primary and one extended partition, which can then contain multiple logical partitions. MBR disks are limited to 2TB in size. For modern systems, especially those with larger disks, the GUID Partition Table (GPT) has become the standard. GPT supports virtually unlimited partitions and disk sizes far beyond 2TB, making it the preferred choice for new installations. You'll often encounter disks named `/dev/sda`, `/dev/sdb`, and so on, with partitions like `/dev/sda1`, `/dev/sda2`.

To manage MBR partitions, the `fdisk` utility is your go-to command-line tool. When you run `fdisk /dev/sdb` (replacing `/dev/sdb` with your target disk), you enter an interactive prompt. Here, you can use commands like `p` to print the current partition table, `n` to create a new partition, `d` to delete one, and `w` to write changes to the disk. It's crucial to remember that changes are only applied when you use `w`; until then, they are just in memory. For GPT disks, `gdisk` offers a similar interactive interface, with commands like `p`, `n`, `d`, and `w` functioning in much the same way. A more modern and versatile tool for both MBR and GPT is `parted`, which can be used interactively or non-interactively. For instance, `parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt` initializes a disk with a GPT label, and `parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 1MiB 10GiB` creates a 10GB primary partition. Always exercise extreme caution when modifying partition tables, as incorrect operations can lead to data loss. It's a good practice to back up any critical data before making significant changes to disk partitioning.

Once a partition is created, it needs a filesystem to store data. Linux supports several filesystem types, with XFS being the default for RHEL 7 and later, and ext4 still widely used. XFS is known for its high performance, scalability, and robustness, especially with large files and directories. ext4 is a mature and reliable journaling filesystem. To create a filesystem, you use the `mkfs` command family. For example, `mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1` will format the first partition of `/dev/sdb` with an XFS filesystem. Similarly, `mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb2` will create an ext4 filesystem. After formatting, the filesystem is ready to be mounted. Mounting makes the filesystem accessible at a specific directory, known as a mount point. You can manually mount a filesystem using `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data`, where `/mnt/data` is an existing empty directory. To see currently mounted filesystems, simply run `mount` or `df -h`. When a filesystem is no longer needed, it should be unmounted using `umount /mnt/data` or `umount /dev/sdb1`. Attempting to unmount a filesystem that is in use will result in an error, often indicating "device is busy."

For filesystems to be available automatically after a system reboot, they must be configured in the `/etc/fstab` file. This file lists all filesystems the system should mount at boot time, along with their mount points, filesystem types, mount options, and dump/fsck settings. Each line in `/etc/fstab` represents a single filesystem. A typical entry looks like this: `/dev/sdb1 /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0`. Here, `/dev/sdb1` is the device, `/mnt/data` is the mount point, `xfs` is the filesystem type, `defaults` includes common mount options (like `rw`, `suid`, `dev`, `exec`, `auto`, `nouser`, `async`), and the last two zeros indicate that the filesystem should not be dumped and `fsck` should not check it at boot (for XFS, `fsck` is typically not needed). It's generally safer to use the UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) of a partition instead of its device name in `/etc/fstab`, as device names can change if you add or remove other storage devices. You can find a partition's UUID using `blkid /dev/sdb1`. An `/etc/fstab` entry with a UUID might look like `UUID=abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0`. After modifying `/etc/fstab`, it's crucial to test the configuration without rebooting, using `mount -a`. This command attempts to mount all entries in `/etc/fstab` that are not already mounted. If there are errors, `mount -a` will fail, allowing you to correct them before a reboot potentially renders your system unbootable. Common mistakes include typos in `/etc/fstab`, specifying a non-existent mount point, or using incorrect filesystem types. Always double-check your entries and ensure mount points exist and are empty before attempting to mount.

screens.title: Managing Local Storage with Partitions and Filesystems
screens.subtitle: How disks become usable storage: partition, format, mount, and configure for boot

narration.text: In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of how a physical disk becomes a usable filesystem in RHEL. You will learn why partition tables matter, when to choose MBR or GPT, how to create partitions with command-line tools, how to format those partitions with XFS or ext4, and how to make them available at boot using /etc/fstab. This matters because correct partitioning and fstab entries prevent data loss and avoid unbootable systems. For example, on a modern server with a 4 terabyte disk you must use GPT — trying to use tools designed for MBR will produce errors. You will also see a complete hands-on sequence that starts with making a mount point, partitioning a new disk with gdisk, creating an XFS filesystem, getting its UUID, and adding a safe /etc/fstab entry that you test with mount -a before rebooting. Throughout, we'll highlight common mistakes like using device names instead of UUIDs or trying to unmount a busy mount point. By the end, you'll understand the end-to-end workflow and a safe pattern to follow whenever you add disks to a RHEL system.

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Partition disks, create filesystems, mount them manually, and configure reliable automatic mounts using UUIDs in /etc/fstab.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Managing Local Storage with Partitions and Filesystems

Turn raw disks into mounted, persistent storage. Learn partition selection, file system creation, and safe fstab configuration for reliable reboots.

Partitioning
MBR vs GPT
Formatting
mkfs.xfs, mkfs.ext4
Mounting
mount, /etc/fstab
In this lesson

Coming up

Concept Map
Partition table

Filesystem

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part A
screens.subtitle: Identify partition types and use core partitioning tools

narration.text: These objectives set the skills you will practice in this chapter. First, you will be able to identify and contrast MBR and GPT partitioning schemes, understanding their limits and when to prefer GPT. That includes a clear recognition that MBR is older and limited in partition count and disk size, whereas GPT supports modern large disks. Second, you will learn the command-line tools used to create and manage partitions: fdisk for MBR-style disks, gdisk for GPT, and parted as a flexible option for both. Practically, you will run interactive sessions that use the commands to print tables, create and delete partitions, and write changes. Each objective focuses on safe, reversible steps: we emphasize that partition table edits are not applied until you confirm with the write command, and backing up data is essential. Together these skills let you prepare a raw disk so it can later host a filesystem. As you practice, look out for a common misconception: that device names are permanent — they can change when hardware is added, which is why later we use UUIDs in fstab. Your milestone is to demonstrate creation of a partition on a test disk without harming existing data.

keyIdea.title: Objective focus
keyIdea.text: Differentiate MBR and GPT and confidently use fdisk/gdisk/parted to create and inspect partitions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part B
screens.subtitle: Mounting, UUIDs, and troubleshooting fstab safely

narration.text: These four objectives reinforce practical skills and safety checks you will apply in a lab or production environment. First, you will mount and unmount filesystems both by device and by mount point, and understand error messages like "device is busy". Second, you'll practice creating XFS and ext4 filesystems using the mkfs family of commands and recognize the default filesystem choice on RHEL systems. Third, you will retrieve a partition's UUID with blkid and compose reliable /etc/fstab entries that use UUIDs rather than device names so mounts persist despite device node changes. Finally, you will diagnose common fstab errors and safely test your configuration with mount -a before rebooting. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or check: always create the mount point directory, keep it empty, test with mount -a, and back up critical data before partition changes. Achieving these objectives will prepare you to add a disk, partition it with GPT, format it as XFS, and make it available every boot without risking the system's ability to start.

screens.title: Partitioning concepts: MBR and GPT
screens.subtitle: What each scheme stores and why size limits matter

narration.text: Partitioning divides a physical disk into logical segments the operating system can treat independently. Two partitioning schemes you will encounter are MBR, short for Master Boot Record, and GPT, the GUID Partition Table. MBR stores its partition table in the first 512 bytes of the disk and historically supports up to four primary partitions or three primary plus an extended partition with logical partitions inside it. GPT stores metadata in multiple places on the disk and uses GUIDs for entries, allowing many more partitions and disk sizes well beyond the 2 terabyte limit you find with MBR. In practical terms, if you are working with modern disks larger than 2 TB or systems that require many partitions, choose GPT. A common misconception is that partition tools always change the disk immediately. Interactive tools typically stage edits in memory until you explicitly confirm with the write command; this gives you a chance to review. Example: when a cloud VM shows /dev/sdb as a new disk, you decide whether to apply an MBR or GPT label depending on the disk size and use case. The core takeaway is to pick the partitioning scheme that matches the disk scale and to be deliberate when writing changes to avoid accidental data loss.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: GPT is the modern default for large disks; MBR is limited and primarily for legacy scenarios.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Partitioning Concepts
What is a partition table?

A partition table is metadata that subdivides a disk into entries that operating systems use to find filesystems and boot loaders. MBR and GPT store this metadata differently and impose different limits.

MBR — older, 2 TB limit, up to 4 primary partitions
GPT — modern, many partitions, supports very large disks
Common misconception

Using fdisk on a large disk will fail if the disk exceeds MBR limits; switch to gdisk or parted for GPT operations.

Concrete example

You attach a 4 TB disk to a RHEL VM. fdisk reports the disk is too large. The correct response is to initialize the disk with GPT using gdisk or parted so you can create partitions that span the full 4 TB.

Quick checklist
  • Confirm disk size with lsblk or fdisk -l
  • Choose GPT for >2 TB disks
  • Back up data before changing partition tables
Key Takeaway

Pick GPT for modern large disks; treat partition table writes as a deliberate, confirmed action.

screens.title: Device naming and partition nodes
screens.subtitle: How kernel device names map to partitions like /dev/sdb1

narration.text: Understanding device names helps you avoid mistakes when formatting or mounting storage. In Linux, whole block devices are exposed as names such as /dev/sda, /dev/sdb, and so on. Partitions on those disks are represented by numbers appended to the device node, for example /dev/sdb1 for the first partition, /dev/sdb2 for the second. On devices with names that already include a digit, tools append a 'p' before the number, such as /dev/nvme0n1p1. A common error is to format the whole disk (for example /dev/sdb) instead of a partition (for example /dev/sdb1), which destroys the partition table and any existing data. Another important point is that device names can shift when you add or remove hardware. For this reason, the stable identifier to use in /etc/fstab is the partition UUID rather than a device name. To inspect current device nodes and their partitions use lsblk or fdisk -l; these commands show the mapping so you can confidently choose the correct node to operate on. Always double-check the node and the partition number before running destructive commands like mkfs. Device naming and partition nodes means target partition nodes (e.g., /dev/sdb1) for formatting and mounting; use uuids later in fstab for stability.. In practical terms, how kernel device names map to partitions like /dev/sdb1. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical rule
keyIdea.text: Target partition nodes (e.g., /dev/sdb1) for formatting and mounting; use UUIDs later in fstab for stability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Device Names & Partitions
How names map

Whole disks: /dev/sda, /dev/sdb. Partitions: add a number: /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2. NVMe-style devices include a p separator: /dev/nvme0n1p1.

$ lsblk
NAME   MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
sda      8:0    0  100G  0 disk 
├─sda1   8:1    0   50G  0 part /
└─sda2   8:2    0   50G  0 part /home
sdb      8:16   0    4T  0 disk 
└─sdb1   8:17   0    4T  0 part
Mistake to avoid

Do not run mkfs on /dev/sdb when you mean /dev/sdb1. Destroying the partition table will require recovery steps and likely data loss.

Quick checks before destructive commands
  • Confirm device with lsblk or fdisk -l
  • Ensure partition number exists and is not mounted
  • Back up any important data first
Pro Tip

Use lsblk with -f to view filesystem types and UUIDs when available before formatting.

screens.title: Using fdisk interactively (MBR)
screens.subtitle: Print, create, delete, and write partition changes with fdisk

narration.text: fdisk is a familiar interactive utility for managing MBR-style disks. When you run fdisk against a device, for example fdisk /dev/sdb, you enter a prompt offering single-letter commands. Use p to print the current partition table so you can confirm existing partitions. Use n to create a new partition and follow the prompts for partition number and size. Use d to delete a partition and w to write changes to disk. Importantly, fdisk stages changes in memory until you run w; this gives you an opportunity to review your plan and exit without writing if something looks wrong. A practical example: on a small test disk you might run fdisk /dev/sdb, press n, accept defaults to use the entire disk, then w to write. A common misconception is that fdisk will update partitions live; instead it updates kernel state when the partition table is written, and sometimes you must re-read the partition table or reboot if the kernel does not accept the changes immediately. Always confirm your target device to avoid editing a mounted or system disk. Practice these steps in a controlled environment and back up any important data first.

keyIdea.title: Safe pattern
keyIdea.text: Use p to inspect, n to add, and only commit changes with w after careful review.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › fdisk: MBR workflow
Interactive commands you'll use
p — print partition table
n — new partition
d — delete partition
w — write changes to disk
Remember: fdisk stages changes in memory. If you want to exit without saving, use q. Always verify with p before w.
Example session
$ sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
Command (m for help): p
Disk /dev/sdb: 4 TiB, ...
Command (m for help): n
Partition type: primary
Partition number (1-4): 1
First sector (2048-...): 
Last sector, +sectors or +size{K,M,G,T,P} (2048-...): 
Command (m for help): w
The partition table has been altered.
Common misconception

Assuming fdisk writes immediately — always check before writing. Use q to quit safely.

screens.title: gdisk and parted for GPT disks
screens.subtitle: Tools that handle GPT and large disks reliably

narration.text: For GPT disks, use gdisk or parted. gdisk is interactive much like fdisk but designed for GUID Partition Tables. You use the same kinds of commands — p to print, n to create a partition, d to delete, and w to write changes — but gdisk understands GPT metadata and GUIDs. parted is more modern and can operate both interactively and in scripted, non-interactive modes. For example, parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt will initialize a disk with a GPT label, and parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 1MiB 10GiB creates a primary partition spanning those sectors. A practical choice is to use gdisk when you want an fdisk-like interactive experience on GPT, and use parted when scripting or creating partitions by size in one command. A common pitfall is to mix tools without re-reading the partition table; always confirm with lsblk or partprobe so the kernel sees the latest layout. When working with a new large disk, initialize it with mklabel gpt and then create partitions appropriate for the workload. This approach avoids the 2 TB limit and gives you the flexibility modern systems need.

keyIdea.title: Tool selection
keyIdea.text: Use gdisk for interactive GPT edits and parted for scripted or size-based partitioning; always re-check kernel visibility after writes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › gdisk & parted
gdisk — fdisk for GPT

gdisk offers an interactive prompt with commands similar to fdisk but understands GPT and GUIDs. Use it for manual partitioning on modern disks.

$ sudo gdisk /dev/sdb
Command (? for help): p
Command (? for help): n
Command (? for help): w
parted — scriptable and versatile

parted can create labels and partitions non-interactively. It's suitable for scripting and precise size specifications like 1MiB and 10GiB boundaries.

$ sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
$ sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 1MiB 10GiB
Checklist after writing
  • Run lsblk or fdisk -l to confirm partitions
  • If kernel still shows old layout, use partprobe or reboot
  • Confirm the partition type if required by your workflow

screens.title: Formatting partitions with mkfs
screens.subtitle: Create XFS and ext4 filesystems with mkfs utilities

narration.text: After creating a partition, the next step is to format it with a filesystem so the OS can store files there. On RHEL, XFS is commonly the default for new installations and is valued for performance and scalability. ext4 remains widely used and is a stable journaling filesystem. To create an XFS filesystem on the first partition of /dev/sdb, use the mkfs. xfs command targeting /dev/sdb1. For ext4, use mkfs. ext4 on the target partition. A simple command sequence looks like this: create the partition, then run sudo mkfs. xfs /dev/sdb1. After formatting, verify the filesystem with lsblk -f or blkid which shows the filesystem type and UUID. A common misconception is that formatting occurs on the disk device rather than the partition; always target the partition node to avoid overwriting the partition table. Also remember to create a mount point directory before mounting and to confirm the filesystem is not mounted during formatting. These steps prepare the partition for mounting and for being registered in /etc/fstab using a UUID for stability across reboots and device reordering. Formatting partitions with mkfs means use mkfs.xfs or mkfs.ext4 on partition nodes (e.g., /dev/sdb1), then verify the filesystem type and uuid before mounting.. In practical terms, create xfs and ext4 filesystems with mkfs utilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Formatting rule
keyIdea.text: Use mkfs.xfs or mkfs.ext4 on partition nodes (e.g., /dev/sdb1), then verify the filesystem type and UUID before mounting.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Formatting Filesystems
Common filesystems
XFS — default on many RHEL systems, good for large files
ext4 — mature and reliable journaling filesystem
Always format partitions, not whole disks, and verify with lsblk -f or blkid.
Example commands
$ sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
meta-data=/dev/sdb1 isize=512 agcount=4, agsize=... 
$ sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb2
mke2fs 1.45.5 (07-Jan-2020)
After formatting, run sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to capture the UUID for /etc/fstab entries.
Key Takeaway

Formatting prepares a partition for use. Pick XFS for RHEL default workloads and always verify with blkid or lsblk -f.

screens.title: Mounting and unmounting filesystems
screens.subtitle: Make a filesystem accessible and cleanly detach it

narration.text: Mounting attaches a filesystem to an existing directory so the operating system can read and write files there. The mount command takes a device and a mount point, for example mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data where /mnt/data must exist and be empty. After mounting, tools like mount or df -h will show the mounted filesystem. To detach, use umount with either the mount point or the device: umount /mnt/data or umount /dev/sdb1. A common error is trying to unmount a filesystem that is in use; the kernel will report the device is busy. To debug, check for open files with lsof or fuser and close processes holding the mount. Another important practice is to create persistent mount entries in /etc/fstab so the filesystem mounts at boot. But before editing fstab, make sure the syntax is correct and the mount point exists. A safe pattern is: create the mount point, mount manually to verify, then add a matching /etc/fstab entry and test with mount -a. This prevents surprises at reboot. Mounting and unmounting filesystems means always verify a manual mount before adding it to /etc/fstab; resolve busy devices before unmounting.. In practical terms, make a filesystem accessible and cleanly detach it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mount discipline
keyIdea.text: Always verify a manual mount before adding it to /etc/fstab; resolve busy devices before unmounting.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Mounting & Unmounting
Manual mount steps
$ sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
$ sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
$ df -h /mnt/data
Always ensure the mount point exists and is empty. Use the mount or df commands to confirm the filesystem is accessible.
Clean unmount
$ sudo umount /mnt/data
umount: /mnt/data: device is busy

If the device is busy, run lsof /mnt/data or fuser -m /mnt/data to find processes that must be stopped or detached first.

Check your understanding
  • Why must the mount point directory be empty before mounting?
  • How do you resolve a "device is busy" unmount error?

screens.title: Understanding /etc/fstab entries
screens.subtitle: Fields, mount options, and why UUIDs are preferred

narration.text: The /etc/fstab file describes filesystems that the system should mount automatically at boot. Each line represents one filesystem and contains a device identifier, a mount point, the filesystem type, mount options, and two numeric fields used by dump and fsck. A common example is /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0. However, device names like /dev/sdb1 can change when hardware is added or removed. To avoid this, use the UUID returned by blkid and reference it as UUID=abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 in fstab. The mount options field like defaults expands to common settings, including read-write, user restrictions, and async behavior. The final two zeros usually indicate no dump and no fsck at boot, which is common for XFS. After editing /etc/fstab, always test with mount -a to catch syntax errors or missing mount points before rebooting. A typical mistake is adding an entry for a non-existent mount point or mistyping the filesystem type, which causes mount -a to fail and can lead to boot problems if missed. Use the UUID workflow to keep fstab resilient. Understanding /etc/fstab entries means prefer uuid= entries and always validate new lines with mount -a to detect errors before reboot.. In practical terms, fields, mount options, and why uuids are preferred. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: fstab safety
keyIdea.text: Prefer UUID= entries and always validate new lines with mount -a to detect errors before reboot.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › /etc/fstab explained
Fields in an /etc/fstab line
# device       mountpoint    fstype  options    dump pass
UUID=abcdef...  /mnt/data      xfs     defaults   0    0

The device field can be a UUID or device path. The options field may be defaults or a comma-separated list. The last two fields control dump and fsck behavior.

Why UUIDs?

Device names can reassign when hardware changes. UUIDs are stable identifiers embedded in the filesystem metadata, making fstab robust across device reordering.

Verify after editing
$ sudo mount -a
# will attempt to mount all fstab entries and report errors

screens.title: Retrieving UUIDs with blkid
screens.subtitle: Capture stable identifiers for fstab entries

narration.text: blkid is the command that reports block device attributes including filesystem type and UUID. After formatting a partition, run sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to get a line that includes UUID="abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890" and TYPE="xfs". Copy the UUID into /etc/fstab to ensure the mount persists even if device names change. A practical example: create an XFS filesystem, then run blkid, then append a line to /etc/fstab using echo with the UUID or by editing the file with an editor. Always check that the mount point exists and that the fstab entry references the correct filesystem type; a mismatch will cause mount -a to fail. A typical misconception is that UUIDs are the device serial number; they are generated per filesystem and embedded in its metadata. If you ever need to change a filesystem, creating a new filesystem will also create a new UUID, so remember to update fstab accordingly. Use blkid as your authoritative source when creating stable fstab entries. Retrieving UUIDs with blkid means use blkid after formatting to obtain the uuid and include it in /etc/fstab for stable mounts.. In practical terms, capture stable identifiers for fstab entries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UUID practice
keyIdea.text: Use blkid after formatting to obtain the UUID and include it in /etc/fstab for stable mounts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › blkid & UUIDs
Example output
$ sudo blkid /dev/sdb1
/dev/sdb1: UUID="abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890" TYPE="xfs"

Copy the UUID and reference it in /etc/fstab to avoid dependency on device node names.

Append to /etc/fstab safely
$ echo "UUID=abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 /data/projectX xfs defaults 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
$ sudo mount -a

Testing with mount -a ensures errors are caught before rebooting.

screens.title: Testing /etc/fstab and common errors
screens.subtitle: Use mount -a and debug typical mistakes before reboot

narration.text: Editing /etc/fstab is powerful and risky. A small typo can stop a boot if the system expects a mount that fails. The safe workflow is: create and verify the mount point directory, mount the filesystem manually, then add the matching line to /etc/fstab and run sudo mount -a. mount -a attempts to mount all entries and will report errors, allowing you to fix typos before rebooting. Common errors include specifying the wrong device or UUID, mistyping the filesystem type, or adding a non-existent mount point. Another frequent mistake is relying on device names in fstab instead of UUIDs; when device names change, mounts break. If mount -a fails, read the error message — it commonly points to a missing mount directory or an incorrect UUID. Use journalctl or dmesg if the kernel refuses to mount. The best practice is to test changes in a maintenance window and keep a known-good path to revert fstab edits in case of failure. This protects system availability and your ability to recover without console access. Testing /etc/fstab and common errors means validate fstab edits with mount -a and inspect errors to correct typos before a reboot.. In practical terms, use mount -a and debug typical mistakes before reboot. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Hands-on scenario: Add a new disk and auto-mount
screens.subtitle: Partition with gdisk, format XFS, get UUID, update /etc/fstab, and test

narration.text: Let's walk the full hands-on sequence step by step. You have an unpartitioned disk at /dev/sdb. First, create the mount point: sudo mkdir -p /data/projectX. Next, initialize the disk with GPT using gdisk: run sudo gdisk /dev/sdb, type g to create a GPT label, then n to create a partition and w to write. After partitioning, format the new partition with XFS using sudo mkfs. xfs /dev/sdb1. Now retrieve the partition UUID using sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 and copy it. Append an fstab entry with the UUID, for example echo "UUID=<UUID_FROM_BLKID> /data/projectX xfs defaults 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab. Finally, test the configuration by running sudo mount -a then verify with df -h /data/projectX. A useful check is to reboot in a test environment to confirm persistent mounting. Common pitfalls include forgetting to create the mount point, mistyping the UUID, or not testing with mount -a. This exact sequence protects the running system and ensures the mount persists across reboots. Hands-on scenario: Add a new disk and auto-mount means mkdir → gdisk (g, n, w) → mkfs.xfs → blkid → add uuid to /etc/fstab → mount -a → verify.. screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid mistakes that cause data loss or boot failures

narration.text: This screen collects recurring pitfalls and best practices you should internalize. First, never write partition changes until you have reviewed them; interactive tools stage edits and require a separate write command. Second, avoid formatting the whole disk when you mean to format a partition; confirm nodes with lsblk. Third, prefer UUIDs in /etc/fstab instead of device names because device nodes can change when storage is rearranged. Fourth, always create and verify mount points before adding them to fstab and run mount -a to catch errors. Fifth, when unmounting, resolve busy devices with lsof or fuser rather than forcing unmounts that might corrupt data. A common misconception is that XFS always needs fsck — XFS has a different maintenance model and typical fstab entries use 0 0 for dump and fsck fields. Finally, keep backups and perform these operations in a maintenance window for production systems. These habits reduce the chance of accidental data loss and prevent system boot issues arising from bad fstab entries. Common pitfalls and best practices means review before write, target partitions not whole disks, use uuids, and validate fstab with mount -a.. screens.subtitle: Core terms and their concise meanings

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts you should retain. Partitioning divides a disk into logical regions; choose GPT for modern large disks and MBR only for legacy or small disks. Filesystems such as XFS and ext4 are structures that organize files on a partition; RHEL commonly uses XFS for its performance and scalability. A mount point is simply an empty directory where a filesystem becomes accessible. Each of these terms is practical: use the correct partitioning scheme for disk size, format a partition with mkfs, and mount it at an empty directory. Keep these definitions top of mind as you perform hands-on tasks so your commands match the intended target and effect.
